fact: Mars is home to Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano in the solar system, about two and a half times the height of Everest.
The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth, by about 3.8 centimetres a year.
The nearest star to the Sun is Proxima Centauri, a faint red dwarf about 4.2 light-years away.
A nova happens when a white dwarf pulls gas from a companion star until the gas ignites in a brilliant thermonuclear flash.
The Soviet Union's Luna 2 became the first spacecraft to reach the Moon's surface when it crashed there in 1959.
Vega, one of the brightest stars in the northern sky, became the first star after the Sun to be photographed, in 1850.
A comet's coma is the glowing cloud of gas and dust that forms around its icy nucleus as sunlight warms it.
Most shooting stars are specks of comet dust, many no bigger than a grain of sand, burning up high in the atmosphere.
A ring-shaped halo around the Moon appears when moonlight is bent by ice crystals in high, thin clouds.
Saturn's rings are mostly water ice and, though about 270,000 kilometres across, are in most places less than 100 metres thick.
Ocean tides are raised mostly by the Moon's gravity, with the Sun adding a smaller pull of its own.
Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees, which is why we have seasons.
The Boötes Void is a region roughly 300 million light-years across that holds remarkably few galaxies.
The asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter holds millions of rocks, yet its total mass is only about 3 percent of the Moon's.
The Sun's core reaches about 15 million degrees Celsius, hot enough to fuse hydrogen into helium.
A burn is a planned firing of a spacecraft's engine; Apollo crews used one to leave Earth orbit for the Moon.
In 1975, during the Apollo–Soyuz mission, American and Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit for the first time.
The International Space Station's first resident crew arrived on this day in 2000, and it has been crewed ever since.
The Space Shuttle's giant orange external tank held liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen to feed its three main engines.
NASA's Dawn was the first spacecraft to orbit two different worlds beyond Earth: the giant asteroid Vesta and dwarf planet Ceres.
NASA's Juno reached Jupiter in 2016, becoming the first solar-powered spacecraft to explore the giant planet.
ESA's Gaia mapped the positions and motions of nearly two billion stars before it was switched off in 2025.
Eris, a dwarf planet discovered beyond Pluto in 2005, is slightly smaller than Pluto but more massive.
Crux, the Southern Cross, is the smallest of the 88 modern constellations and never rises above the horizon anywhere in Canada.
The James Webb Space Telescope, which holds its aim using Canada's Fine Guidance Sensor, launched on this day in 2021.
Anik A1, launched in 1972, made Canada the first country with its own domestic communications satellite in geostationary orbit.
The International Space Station circles Earth about every 90 minutes, so its crew sees around 16 sunrises a day.
A comet's tail always points away from the Sun, pushed by sunlight and the solar wind rather than trailing behind.
Six Apollo landings brought back about 382 kilograms of lunar rock and soil, still studied by scientists today.
NASA's Parker Solar Probe became the fastest human-made object in 2024, passing the Sun at about 690,000 kilometres per hour.
Sojourner became the first rover on Mars in 1997, rolling off NASA's Pathfinder lander for a mission planned to last a week.
The nadir is the point directly beneath you; Earth-observation satellites usually point their cameras toward it.
NASA's New Horizons flew past Pluto on this day in 2015, revealing a vast heart-shaped region on its surface.
Soyuz spacecraft have carried crews since 1967, making Soyuz the longest-serving crewed spacecraft design in history.
An Atlas rocket launched John Glenn in 1962, making him the first American to orbit Earth.
The solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun, flows past Earth at hundreds of kilometres per second.
A solar flare is a sudden burst of radiation from the Sun; strong ones can disrupt radio signals on Earth's daytime side.
Rockets shed empty stages as they climb so they stop carrying dead weight; the Saturn V Moon rocket had three.
In 2018 a Soyuz rocket failed on its way to orbit, and the capsule's escape system brought both crew members home safely.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that astronomers have watched continuously since the 1800s.
Spacewalkers' helmet visors carry a microscopically thin layer of gold that reflects the Sun's heat and glare.
The International Space Station's long truss is its backbone, holding the solar arrays and radiators away from the crew modules.
Voyager 2 is still the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune, flying past them in 1986 and 1989.
A white dwarf is the Earth-sized leftover core of a star like the Sun; one teaspoon of it would weigh tonnes.
In about five billion years the Sun will swell into a red giant, swallowing Mercury and Venus.
The umbra is the darkest part of a shadow; only people standing in the Moon's umbra see a total solar eclipse.
Canada's RADARSAT satellites use radar to image Earth through cloud and darkness, tracking sea ice for ships and the Coast Guard.
Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the Moon that observatories still hit with lasers to measure its distance to within centimetres.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, so we always see the Sun as it was moments ago.
A satellite in polar orbit passes over both poles, letting it scan the entire planet as Earth turns beneath it.
Space is commonly said to begin at the Kármán line, 100 kilometres above sea level, though the United States uses 80.
The Sun's activity rises and falls over a cycle of about 11 years, swinging from few sunspots to many.
Cassini flew through plumes of water vapour and ice spraying from cracks near the south pole of Saturn's moon Enceladus.
Earth is the densest planet in the solar system, thanks largely to its heavy iron core.
Venus spins backwards, and so slowly that one turn on its axis takes longer than its whole trip around the Sun.
Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and the only dwarf planet in the inner solar system.
Saturn's moon Titan has a thick atmosphere and lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane on its surface.
NASA's Orion capsule launched on this day in 2026, carrying Artemis II's four astronauts, including Canada's Jeremy Hansen, around the Moon.
Rigel, the brilliant blue-white star at Orion's foot, gives off tens of thousands of times more light than the Sun.
Spica, the brightest star in Virgo, is really two hot stars so close together that they orbit each other every four days.
Vesta is the brightest asteroid seen from Earth and, under very dark skies, can occasionally be spotted with the naked eye.
OSIRIS-REx returned a sample of asteroid Bennu in 2023, and Canada earned 4 percent of it by building the mission's laser altimeter.
Eagle was Apollo 11's lunar module, the craft that set Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin down in the Sea of Tranquility.
NASA's MAVEN orbiter spent over 11 years at Mars studying how the planet lost much of its atmosphere to space.
Canada's CHIME radio telescope in British Columbia has detected thousands of fast radio bursts, brief flashes mostly from other galaxies.
The zenith is the point in the sky directly overhead, exactly opposite the nadir beneath your feet.
Pulsars are spinning neutron stars; the first was discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell, then a graduate student at Cambridge.
Quasars are the blazing centres of distant galaxies, powered by gas spiralling into supermassive black holes.
A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space; many, like the Orion Nebula, are nurseries where stars form.
The Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away, is the most distant object most people can see with the naked eye.
Auroras glow when charged particles from the Sun strike gases high in Earth's atmosphere; oxygen produces the common green.
Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on this day in 1969, and Apollo missions went on to put twelve astronauts on its surface.
Dextre, Canada's two-armed robot for delicate maintenance work on the International Space Station, launched on this day in 2008.
NASA's Kepler space telescope discovered more than 2,600 planets beyond our solar system during its nine years of work.
In 2015 SpaceX's Falcon 9 made the first landing of an orbital rocket's booster, and its boosters now routinely fly again.
Craters on the Moon can last billions of years because it has no wind, rain or plate tectonics to wear them away.
A meteor is the streak of light from a space rock burning up in the air; a piece that lands is a meteorite.
In 2006 astronomers defined a planet as a round body orbiting the Sun that has cleared its orbit of other objects.
A rocket works in the vacuum of space because it pushes against its own exhaust, not against the air.
Rockets often launch eastward to borrow speed from Earth's rotation, which is fastest at the equator.
The Saturn V's five first-stage engines produced about 7.6 million pounds of thrust at liftoff.
A satellite in an elliptical orbit moves slowest at apogee, its farthest point from Earth.
The Sun's corona, its outer atmosphere, is hundreds of times hotter than the visible surface below it, a long-standing puzzle.
A parsec, about 3.26 light-years, is the distance at which a star's parallax, its apparent shift as Earth orbits, is one arcsecond.
Plasma, gas so hot its atoms lose their electrons, is the most common state of ordinary matter in the visible universe.
In 2016 a speck of orbital debris, probably a fleck of paint, chipped a seven-millimetre crater in a space station window.
The Cupola, a dome of seven windows added to the International Space Station in 2010, gives astronauts their best view of Earth.
The Soviet Venera 7 lander became the first spacecraft to send data from the surface of another planet, Venus, in 1970.
Algol, the Demon Star of Perseus, dims every 2.87 days as the fainter star of a binary pair passes in front.
Sound cannot travel through the near-perfect vacuum of space, because there is almost nothing there to carry it.
Spacewalkers stay clipped to the station by safety tethers so they cannot drift away into space.
Saturn's average density is lower than water's, so in a big enough bathtub the planet would float.
Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side, its axis tilted about 98 degrees.
Jupiter's moon Europa may hide a salty ocean beneath its ice; NASA's Europa Clipper launched in 2024 to investigate.
Sirius, the Dog Star, is the brightest star in the night sky and lies about 8.6 light-years away.
The Carina Nebula's Cosmic Cliffs were among the first images from the James Webb Space Telescope, released in July 2022.
Vostok 1 carried Yuri Gagarin on the first human spaceflight on this day in 1961, a single orbit of Earth.
The Hubble Space Telescope launched aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery on this day in 1990.
Skylab, the first American space station, launched in 1973 and hosted three crews before the last one left in 1974.
Total solar eclipses happen because the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and also about 400 times farther away.
A rocket's payload, the satellite, cargo or crew it carries, is usually only a small fraction of its weight at liftoff.
Perigee is the point of an orbit closest to Earth; a full moon near perigee is popularly called a supermoon.
Neptune was the first planet found by mathematical prediction: astronomers calculated where it should be before spotting it in 1846.
Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, launched on this day in 1957.
NASA's Artemis I launched on this day in 2022, sending an uncrewed Orion capsule on a trip around the Moon.
Voyager 1 launched on this day in 1977, and in 2012 it became the first spacecraft to reach interstellar space.
The Cassini spacecraft launched on this day in 1997 and went on to orbit Saturn for 13 years.
Crew capsules return from space blunt end first, so a heat shield takes the fierce heat of plunging through the air.
Astronauts leave the space station through an airlock, a small chamber emptied of air so the rest of the station stays sealed.
The International Space Station is the largest structure humans have built in space, spreading over about a football field.
NASA's Space Shuttle flew 135 missions between 1981 and 2011, launching like a rocket and landing like a glider.
NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter carries HiRISE, a camera that can spot features on Mars as small as a kitchen table.
The Space Shuttle's two solid rocket boosters parachuted into the Atlantic after launch and were recovered, refurbished and flown again.
During reentry, air in front of a capsule grows so hot it turns to plasma, which can briefly block radio contact with the crew.
Liftoff happens only once a rocket's thrust is greater than its weight, which is why rockets rise slowly before speeding up.
Gravity on the Moon is about one sixth of Earth's, which is why Apollo astronauts could bound across its surface.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a ball only about 20 kilometres across.
A black hole's event horizon is the boundary beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape.
Most known exoplanets were found by the transit method, which watches for a star dimming slightly as a planet crosses in front.
At each equinox, in March and September, the Sun crosses the celestial equator and day and night are nearly equal everywhere.
Sunspots look dark only because they are cooler than the surface around them, though they are still thousands of degrees.
A gibbous moon is more than half lit but not yet full, a phase it passes through twice each month.
Stellar means 'of the stars', and most elements heavier than helium were forged inside stars or in their explosive deaths.
NEOSSAT, a suitcase-sized Canadian space telescope that hunts asteroids and tracks satellites, launched on this day in 2013.
Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets in the solar system combined.
Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so its surface swings from about 430 °C by day to about −180 °C at night.
Polaris, the North Star, sits almost directly above Earth's North Pole, so it barely moves while other stars circle around it.
ESA's Rosetta orbited comet 67P and released the Philae lander, which made the first landing on a comet in 2014.
Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and the first to fly past Jupiter, in 1973.
Telstar 1 launched on this day in 1962 and soon relayed the first live television pictures across the Atlantic.
